'''''Plumeria rubra''''' is a [[deciduous]] plant species belonging to the genus ''[[Plumeria]]''.<ref name="Botanica 691">"Botanica. The Illustrated AZ of over 10000 garden plants and how to cultivate them", p. 691. Könemann, 2004. {{ISBN|3-8331-1253-0}}</ref> Originally native to [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], [[Colombia]] and [[Venezuela]], it has been widely cultivated in subtropical and tropical climates worldwide and is a popular garden and park plant, as well as being used in temples and cemeteries. It grows as a spreading tree to {{convert|7|–|8|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and wide, and is flushed with fragrant flowers of shades of pink, white and yellow over the summer and autumn.

Its common names include '''frangipani''',<ref name="GRIN" /> '''red paucipan''',<ref name="GRIN" /> '''red-jasmine''',<ref name="GRIN" /> '''red frangipani''', '''common frangipani,''' '''temple tree''',<ref name="GRIN" /> '''calachuchi''',<ref name="Bolton">{{cite book |editor1-last=Bolton |editor1-first=Kingsley |editor2-last=Kachru |editor2-first=Braj B. |title=World Englishes Critical Concepts in Linguistics· Volume 3 |date=2006 |publisher=Routledge |location=London |isbn=978-0-415-31508-1 |page=361}}</ref> or simply '''plumeria'''. Despite its common name, the species is not a [[Jasmine#Other plants called "jasmine"|"true jasmine"]] and not of the genus [[Jasmine|''Jasminum'']].

== Taxonomy ==
''Plumeria rubra'' was one of the many species first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]], and appeared in the 1753 edition of ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. Its specific epithet is derived from the [[Latin]] ''ruber'' "red". The epithets ''acuminata'', ''acutifolia'', and ''lutea'' are seen, but these are invalid.

==Common names==
The common name "frangipani" comes from the Italian [[Frangipani family]], a sixteenth-century [[marquess]] of which invented a plumeria-scented perfume. The genus name honors [[Charles Plumier]], who was a French monk of the Franciscan order, and a botanist.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=d451|title=Plumeria rubra - Plant Finder|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org|access-date=2019-04-04}}</ref>

In its native range in [[Mexico]] the common name is {{lang|nah|cacaloxochitl}} or {{lang|nah|cacaloxuchitl}}. The name comes from Nahuatl and means "crow's flower".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.medicinatradicionalmexicana.unam.mx/monografia.php?l=3&t=&id=7302 |title=Biblioteca |publisher=Medicinatradicionalmexicana.unam.mx |access-date=2013-07-12}}</ref> It is also commonly known in Mexico as Flor de Mayo. ''P. rubra'' was declared the national flower of [[Nicaragua]] in 1971, where it is known as {{lang|es|sacuanjoche}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.asamblea.gob.ni/simbolos-nacionales/|title=Simbolos Nacionales|access-date=2017-09-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171006054141/http://www.asamblea.gob.ni/simbolos-nacionales/|archive-date=2017-10-06}}</ref> In Spanish, frangipanis are also referred to as {{lang|es|alhelí}}, {{lang|es|alhelí cimarrón}}, and {{lang|es|suche}}.<ref name=":4">{{cite web|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=28884|title=Taxonomy - GRIN-Global Web v 1.10.4.0|website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=2019-04-04}}</ref> 

''P. rubra'' entered [[Southeast Asia]] via the [[Manila galleons]] from Mexico to the [[Philippines]] in the 1560s.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Noel  |last1=Amano |first2=Greg |last2=Bankoff |first3=David Max |last3=Findley  |first4=Grace |last4=Barretto-Tesoro |first5=Patrick|last5=Roberts |title=Archaeological and historical insights into the ecological impacts of pre-colonial and colonial introductions into the Philippine Archipelago |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0959683620941152 |date=Feb 2021 |journal=[[The Holocene]] |volume=31 |issue=2 |page=320 |doi=10.1177/0959683620941152}}</ref> It retained the Nahuatl-derived name in the [[Philippine languages]] where it is known as {{lang|fil|[[wikt:kalachuchi|kalachuchi]]}} (also spelled {{lang|fil|kalatsutsi}}), or {{lang|en|[[wikt:calachuchi|calachuchi]]}} in [[Philippine English]].<ref name="Bolton"/><ref name="Zumbroich">{{cite journal |last1=Zumbroich |first1=Thomas J. |title='Plumerias the Color of Roseate Spoonbills' -Continuity and transition in the symbolism of ''Plumeria'' L. in Mesoamerica |journal=Ethnobotany Research & Applications |date=2013 |volume=11 |pages=341–363}}</ref> The Nahuatl name is also partly preserved in the [[Ternate]] common name {{lang|tft|tsjutsju}}, derived from the Philippine name.<ref name="Zumbroich"/> In other parts of Indonesia and Malaysia, it acquired different names like {{langx|ms|cempaka}} derived from the resemblance of its fragrance to the [[Magnolia champaca|champaca tree]]; it also acquired the name {{lang|ms|bunga kemboja}} (literally "flower of [[Cambodia]]") in Malay invoking its foreign origin, though there is none evidence of its spread from Cambodia. Due to its associations with [[maqbara|graveyards]] and death, it is also known as {{lang|ms|bunga kuburan}}, literally "grave flower".<ref name="Zumbroich"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Plumeria rubra |url=https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/3/0/3074 |website=Flora and Fauna Web |publisher=Government of Singapore |access-date=7 March 2024}}</ref>

In the [[Pacific Islands]] where it was introduced in the late 19th century,<ref name="Zumbroich"/> ''P. rubra'' is known as {{lang|haw|melia}} in [[Hawaii]],<ref name="ctahr">{{cite web|url=http://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/OF-24.pdf|title=Ornamentals and Flowers OF-24: Plumeria|last=Criley, Richard A|date=February 1998|work=Cooperative Extension Service, C/T/A/H/R|publisher=Department of Horticulture, College of Tropical Agriculture & Human Resources, University of hawaii at Manoa|access-date=31 January 2010}}</ref> and {{lang|rar|tipani}} in the [[Cook Islands]].<ref name=":0"/>

Elsewhere, it is known as ''champa'' (or a derivative thereof) in [[India]] and [[Pakistan]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/1800011|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name - Plumeria rubra L.|website=www.tropicos.org|access-date=2019-03-21}}</ref>  It is known by many names in Brazil, including {{lang|pt|jasmim-de-caiena}}, {{lang|pt|jasmim-do-pará}}, and {{lang|pt|jasmim-manga}}.<ref name=":4" /> In Portuguese, it is also known as {{lang|pt|flor-de-Santo-Antônio}}.<ref name=":4" /> In Cambodia it is given the names {{transliteration|km|châmpéi krahâ:m}} (also romanised as {{transliteration|km|krahom}}, meaning 'red'), or {{transliteration|km|châmpéi slük sruëch}}, while the French term for the species is {{lang|fr|frangipanier à fleurs rouges}}.<ref name=dyphon>Dy Phon Pauline, 2000, ''Plants Used In Cambodia'', printed by Imprimerie Olympic, Phnom Penh.</ref>  In Sri Lanka, it is known as {{transliteration|si|araliya}} in Sinhalese. In Myanmar, it is referred to as {{transliteration|my|mawk-sam-ka}}, {{transliteration|my|mawk-sam-pailong}}, and {{transliteration|my|sonpabataing}}.<ref name=":5">{{cite web|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3169674|title=Plumeria rubra L.|website=www.gbif.org|language=en|access-date=2019-04-04}}</ref> In China, it has the common name {{transliteration|zh|ji dan hua}}, and in the United States, it is referred to as ''nosegay''.<ref name=":0" />

==Description==
''Plumeria rubra'' belongs to the dogbane family and grows as a spreading shrub or small tree to a height of {{convert|2|–|8|m|ft|round=5|abbr=on}} and similar width.<ref name=":2" /> It has a thick succulent trunk and sausage-like blunt branches covered with a thin grey bark. The branches are somewhat brittle and when broken, ooze a white latex that can be irritating to the skin and mucous membranes. This latex found in the stem of the plants is in fact toxic, but not deadly unless present in large quantities.<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Plumeria+rubra|title=Plumeria rubra - Useful Tropical Plants|website=tropical.theferns.info|access-date=2019-04-04}}</ref> The large green leaves can reach {{convert|30|to|50|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and are arranged alternately and clustered at the end of the branches. The boles of these plants can be up to 25 cm in the wild. It tends to be smaller in cultivation.<ref name=":3" />

They are deciduous, falling in the cooler months of the year. The flowers are terminal, appearing at the ends of branches over the summer. Often profuse and very prominent, they are strongly fragrant, and have five petals. The flowers give off their fragrance in the morning and in the evening,. The sweet fragrance functions as an attractant of hawkmoths, the primary pollinators of the species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Steven D. |last2=Moré |first2=Marcela |last3=Amorim |first3=Felipe W. |last4=Haber |first4=William A. |last5=Frankie |first5=Gordon W. |last6=Stanley |first6=Dara A. |last7=Cocucci |first7=Andrea A. |last8=Raguso |first8=Robert A. |date=2017 |title=The long and the short of it: a global analysis of hawkmoth pollination niches and interaction networks |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48582299 |journal=Functional Ecology |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=101–115 |issn=0269-8463}}</ref> This fragrance is similar to that of rose, citrus, and cinnamon.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal|last=Joulain|first=Daniel|date=2008|title=Flower Scents from the Pacific|journal=Chemistry & Biodiversity|language=en|volume=5|issue=6|pages=896–909|doi=10.1002/cbdv.200890103|pmid=18618387|s2cid=12346104|issn=1612-1880}}</ref> The colors range from the common pink to white with shades of yellow in the centre of the flower.<ref name="Botanica 691"/><ref name="UFL">{{cite web|url=http://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/database/documents/pdf/tree_fact_sheets/pluruba.pdf|title=Fact Sheet ST-491 ''Plumeria rubra'' Frangipani|author1=Gilman, Edward F. |author2=Watson, Dennis G. |date=October 1994|work=Environmental Horticulture website|publisher=University of Florida|access-date=22 July 2013|location=Gainesville, FL}}</ref> Initially tubular before opening out, the flowers are {{convert|5|-|7.5|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter, and only rarely go on to produce seed - 20-60 winged seeds are contained in a {{convert|17.5|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} pod.<ref name="ctahr"/> The tubular corolla is well-suited for the elongated proboscides of the hawkmoth, allowing successful pollen transfer during visits of the flowers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Haber |first=William A. |date=1984 |title=Pollination by Deceit in a Mass-Flowering Tropical Tree Plumeria rubra L. (Apocynaceae) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2387935 |journal=Biotropica |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=269–275 |doi=10.2307/2387935 |issn=0006-3606}}</ref> The fruits are cylindrical pods that are rarely found in cultivation.<ref name=":2" />

== Pollination ==
The ''Plumeria Rubra'' species is primarily pollinated by [[Sphingidae|hawkmoths]]. The flowers produce a strong fragrance that becomes more prominent in the evening and nighttime, aligning with the period of greatest hawkmoth activity. Although the flowers attract [[Pollinator|pollinators]] through fragrance and appearance, they actually produce little to no nectar, a pollination strategy known as deceptive pollination.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Steven D. |last2=Moré |first2=Marcela |last3=Amorim |first3=Felipe W. |last4=Haber |first4=William A. |last5=Frankie |first5=Gordon W. |last6=Stanley |first6=Dara A. |last7=Cocucci |first7=Andrea A. |last8=Raguso |first8=Robert A. |date=2017 |title=The long and the short of it: a global analysis of hawkmoth pollination niches and interaction networks |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48582299 |journal=Functional Ecology |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=101–115 |issn=0269-8463}}</ref>

While searching for nectar, the hawkmoths insert their long proboscides into the flower's tubular corolla, where they come into contact with the reproductive structures of the flower and transfer pollen. Studies have reported several hawkmoths carrying ''Plumeria'' flower pollen, demonstrating their role as effective pollinators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Haber |first=William A. |date=1984 |title=Pollination by Deceit in a Mass-Flowering Tropical Tree Plumeria rubra L. (Apocynaceae) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2387935 |journal=Biotropica |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=269–275 |doi=10.2307/2387935 |issn=0006-3606}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Steven D. |last2=Moré |first2=Marcela |last3=Amorim |first3=Felipe W. |last4=Haber |first4=William A. |last5=Frankie |first5=Gordon W. |last6=Stanley |first6=Dara A. |last7=Cocucci |first7=Andrea A. |last8=Raguso |first8=Robert A. |date=2017 |title=The long and the short of it: a global analysis of hawkmoth pollination niches and interaction networks |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48582299 |journal=Functional Ecology |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=101–115 |issn=0269-8463}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Flowers of Plumeria rubra in West Bengal, India.jpg|thumb|Flower of ''Plumeria rubra'' in [[West Bengal]], India.]]
Its native range extends from [[Baja California Peninsula|Baja California]] into central Mexico south through Central America (Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, Belize, Honduras, Panama) to the [[Antioquia Department|Department of Antioquia]] in Colombia and Venezuela in [[South America]].<ref name=":0" /> It is cultivated widely in tropical and subtropical regions of the world, and has become naturalized in most parts of tropical Asia and the Pacific Islands.<ref name="mahr">{{cite web |last1=Mahr |first1=Susan |title=Plumeria |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/plumeria/ |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |publisher=University of Wisconsin-Madison |access-date=7 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="GRIN" /><ref name=":22">{{cite journal|last1=Rebman|first1=J. P.|last2=Gibson|first2=J.|last3=Rich|first3=K.|date=2016|title=Annotated checklist of the vascular plants of Baja California, Mexico|url=http://sdplantatlas.org/pdffiles/BajaChecklist2016.pdf|journal=San Diego Society of Natural History|volume=45|page=39}}</ref> 

''P. rubra'' was introduced in the 1560s into the Philippines during the [[Spanish colonial period of the Philippines|Spanish colonial period]]. From there, it spread to the rest of [[Southeast Asia]] and into other parts of the Asia. It was also introduced into the [[Pacific Islands]] in the late 19th century, where it has since become iconic due to their use in [[Lei (garland)|lei]]s.<ref name="Zumbroich"/>

''P. rubra'' generally inhabits hot and rocky areas with dry to moderate rainfall. They can survive in locations with prominent dry seasons, where they can flower on the bare branches, or in more humid conditions, where they can remain evergreen. It can also be found in rocky forests, mountain slopes, and even occasionally on plains or savannas. It occupies elevations from sea level to 1000 meters but can be found up to elevations of 1500 meters.<ref name=":3" />

==Cultivation==
[[File:Plumeria Rubra Flower.jpg|thumb|A flowering ''Plumeria rubra'' in [[Piracicaba]], [[Brazil]]. ]]
The species is cultivated around the world in subtropical and tropical climates. In Australia, it is widely seen in cultivation in Sydney and Perth and warmer frost free climates northwards.<ref name="ABC">{{cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1653931.htm|title=Fact Sheet: Frangipani|last=Campbell, Colin|date=June 3, 2006|work=Gardening Australia Website|publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation|access-date=31 January 2010}}</ref> In the mainland [[United States]], it tolerates USDA Hardiness zones 10B to 11 (southern coastal [[California]] and the southern tip of [[Florida]]).<ref name="UFL"/> It is also grown in Hawaii to an altitude of 2000 m.<ref name="ctahr"/> They tolerate a wide variety of soils, from acid to alkaline and sandy to clay.<ref name="UFL"/> These plants grow best in dry to medium moisture, well-drained soils in full sun and will bloom through most of the year in tropical areas. They do not grow well in wet soils and in areas with temperatures below {{convert|10|C|F|abbr=on}} during the winter seasons, the plants will stop blooming and shed their leaves.<ref name=":2"/> Established plants are also very salt tolerant and tolerate even salt-laden winds.<ref name=":3"/> Widely available in nurseries, frangipanis are readily propagated by cuttings of branches taken in cooler months and left to dry for a week or more.<ref name="ABC"/> As well as gardens and street- and park planting, frangipanis are planted in temples and cemeteries.<ref name="ctahr"/>

''Plumeria rubra'' is an important crop in [[Hawaii]], with over 14 million flowers sold to be used in [[Lei (Hawaii)|leis]] there in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.actahort.org/members/showpdf?booknrarnr=813_23 |title=Plumeria Rubra: An Old Ornamental, A New Crop |publisher=Actahort.org |access-date=2013-07-12}}</ref>

In [[temperate climate|temperate]] areas ''P. rubra'' must be grown under glass, in a large conservatory or similar, due to its requirement for warm conditions. However it may be placed outside in a sheltered sunny spot during the summer months. In the United Kingdom it has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94126/Plumeria-rubra/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Plumeria rubra''
| access-date = 8 May 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 80 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 7 May 2018}}</ref>

Some forms in cultivation are hybrids between this species and ''[[Plumeria obtusa]]''; these have rounded rather than pointed leaves and are less likely to be deciduous.<ref name="ctahr"/> The white and yellow flowered "Singapore" cultivar, also from the United States, usually holds its leaves all year round in Hawaii.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6MvFZ1P71GQC&q=Hawaii+plumeria+%22all+year%22&pg=PA65|title=Plants and Animals of Hawaii |last=Scott|first=Susan|year=1991|publisher=Bess Press|page=65|isbn=0-935848-93-2|access-date=5 February 2010}}</ref>

''[[Coleosporium]] plumeriae'', known as plumeria rust or frangipani rust, is a fungus which attacks young leaves of ''P. rubra''. It causes a brownish or orange powdery coating or blistering of leaves. It has been recorded from Hawaii and the east coast of Australia.<ref name="ctahr"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.burkesbackyard.com.au/2001/archives/2001_archives/in_the_garden/weeds_and_garden_pests/frangipani_rust|title=Weeds and Garden Pests: Frangipani Rust|last=Burke|first=Don|year=2001|work=Burke's Backyard website|publisher=CTC Productions|access-date=4 February 2010|location=Sydney, Australia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100822171331/http://www.burkesbackyard.com.au/2001/archives/2001_archives/in_the_garden/weeds_and_garden_pests/frangipani_rust|archive-date=22 August 2010}}</ref> It was first recognised by the French mycologist [[Narcisse Théophile Patouillard]] on [[Guadeloupe]] Island in the eastern [[Caribbean]] in 1902, and had reached [[Taiwan]] by 2005.<ref>{{cite web |author=S J Roberts |url=http://www.bspp.org.uk/publications/new-disease-reports/ndr.php?id=011016 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120721150243/http://www.bspp.org.uk/publications/new-disease-reports/ndr.php?id=011016 |archive-date=2012-07-21 |title=The first report of Plumeria (Frangipani) rust disease caused by Coleosporium plumeriae in Taiwan |publisher=Bspp.org.uk |access-date=2013-07-12 }}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Florence Iwalani Koanui (a0006927).jpg|thumb|Florence Iwalani Koanui with Lei from white and yellow ''pua melia'']]
The USDA Forestry Service lists ''Plumeria rubra'' as a poisonous plant and warns against touching or eating any part of the plant.<ref>The USDA Forestry Service's [https://web.archive.org/web/20200712115128/https://www.fs.usda.gov/wps/portal/fsinternet/cs/detail/!ut/p/z1/04_Sj9CPykssy0xPLMnMz0vMAfIjo8zijQwgwNHCwN_DI8zPyBcqYKAfjlVBmA9cQRQx-g1wAEci9eNREIXf-HD9KKxWIPuAkBkFuaGhEQaZjgCVqf1Y/dz/d5/L2dBISEvZ0FBIS9nQSEh/?position=Not%20Yet%20Determined.Html&pname=Forest%20Service%20-%20Nature&ss=110819&navtype=BROWSEBYSUBJECT&pnavid=150000000000000&navid=150130000000000&ttype=detail&cid=fsbdev3_043022 Site for El Yunque National Forest].</ref>

In [[Cambodia]], as with other ''Plumeria'' species, ''P. rubra'' flowers is used for necklaces, as offerings to deities or as decoration for coffins. The leaves of this species are used in the care of sores and made into soothing infusions.<ref name=dyphon />
The flowers and bark of it are also used in traditional [[Chinese medicine]] in the treatment of [[fever]], [[bacillary dysentery]], [[pertussis]] and so on.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Plumeria rubra|title=Plumeria rubra|url=http://www.flowersview.com/Plumeria%20rubra/Plumeria+rubra+%2883%29.jpg.html|website=Flower View}}</ref> Chinese herbal teas such as [[Wang Lao Ji]] also contain P. rubra.

''P. rubra'' possesses fulvoplumierin, an antibiotic that inhibits the growth of ''[[Mycobacterium tuberculosis]]''. The plant has also been shown to be an antifungal, antiviral, analgesic, antispasmodic, and hypoglycemic.<ref name=":3" /> ''P. rubra'' is also reported to contain agoniadin, plumierid, plumeric acid, cerotinic acid, and [[lupeol]], and the stem possesses an alkaloid called triterpinoid. The plant has been known to promote digestion and excretion, along with respiratory and immune functions. The sap of the plant is used as a laxative and is a remedy for bloating and stomachaches. The bark is said to be purgative and is also used for venereal sores. The flowers can be boiled in water or juice and made into a salad to promote bowel movement, urine flow, and to control gas and phlegm. The flowers are also used in the treatment of asthma.<ref name=":5" />

On the Molokai island in the Hawaiian archipelago, ''P. rubra'' is cultivated in order to produce neck garlands ([[lei (garland)|lei]]s).<ref name=":1" /> They are also used to make a scented oil in many Pacific islands that include Hawaii.<ref name=":2" /> The flowers are used to scent coconut oil. The bark contains faint purplish streaks and the wood is hard and compact with a very fine texture. The wood takes a high polish.<ref name=":3" />

== As a symbol ==
''Plumeria rubra'' is the [[National symbols of Nicaragua|national flower of Nicaragua]], where it is known under the local name ''sacuanjoche'', as well as of [[National symbols of Laos|Laos]], where it is known under the local name ''dok champa''. It is also used as the logo of [[Lao Airlines]], the national airline of Laos. <ref>{{cite web |last1=Smart |first1=Bryony |title=Frangipani |url=https://www.pha-tad-ke.com/frangipani/ |website=Pha Tad Ke Botanical Garden |access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref>

''Plumeria rubra'' is also the [[Villages of Guam|village]] flower of [[Asan-Maina, Guam|Asan-Maina]] on [[Guam]].

''Plumeria rubra'' also has great symbolic value in both Hinduism and Buddhism. In Hinduism, it connotes both devotion and eternity, and as such, is often planted near Hindu temples. Within the temples themselves, the flowers are often placed at the feet of statues of various gods. ''Plumeria rubra'' can also be found as part of the landscaping of Buddhist temples. Since the flower renews itself in all kinds of weather, it connotes rebirth.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plumeria Symbolism in Hinduism and Buddhism |url=https://plumerist.com/plumeria-symbolism-hinduism-buddhism/}}</ref>
